short: In 212 CE Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to nearly every free inhabitant of the empire, ending centuries of graduated status.
full:
In 212, the emperor Caracalla issued the Constitutio Antoniniana, extending Roman citizenship to almost all free men within the empire's borders and citizen rights to their wives. Citizenship had until then spread only gradually, through colonies, veteran discharge and individual grants, leaving most provincials as free non-citizens (peregrini) governed by local or customary law rather than Roman law directly.

The edict's surviving text, preserved on a damaged papyrus, states no single motive, though the historian Cassius Dio linked it to revenue: citizens paid inheritance and manumission taxes that peregrini did not. Whatever the intent, the distinction between citizen and subject that had structured Roman law for centuries collapsed at a stroke, and Roman law became, in principle, the law of everyone the empire governed.
